Land
LAND
n. (ground, territory, country; especially the land of promise given to Abraham's seed and held of the LORD as its Owner; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'erets, 'adamah and Greek gē, chōra)
From Old English land, common Germanic, ground or defined territory. Hebrew 'erets is the great word of the Old Testament for both earth and land — context alone decides whether the whole globe or one country is meant — while 'adamah is the tilled soil, the arable ground from which man was taken and to which he returns. Greek gē covers the same range. English keeps a trace of the covenant sense in landed, landlord, and inheritance language generally.

Biblical Definition

Land is the second great promise of the Abrahamic covenant, standing beside seed and blessing: “Get thee out of thy country... unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). Canaan is given, but never sold outright, because the title never leaves God's hands: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Lev 25:23). Israel holds it as a tenant, which is the ground of the whole jubilee legislation, of the sabbath years for the soil, and of the prophets' fury at those who join field to field. The land is also morally responsive: it is defiled by bloodshed and idolatry and vomits out its inhabitants (Lev 18:25–28), and it is watched continually by its Owner — “the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it” (Deu 11:12). Exile is therefore not a political accident but a covenant sanction. The New Testament does not discard the promise; it enlarges it. Abraham himself lived in the land of promise as in a strange country (Heb 11:9), looking past it for a city with foundations, and Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he should be the heir of the world (Rom 4:13). The meek inherit the earth, and the land promise terminates on a renewed creation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Ground or territory; in Scripture, chiefly the land of promise given to Abraham's seed and held as tenants of the LORD who owns it — a possession forfeited by covenant unfaithfulness and enlarged in Christ to the whole renewed earth.

expand to see more

LAND, n. [Sax. land, lond.] 1. Earth, or the solid matter which constitutes the fixed part of the surface of the globe, in distinction from the sea or other waters.

2. Any portion of the solid, superficial part of the globe, whether a kingdom or country, or a particular region. The united provinces of Holland are a rich land.

3. Ground; soil, or the superficial part of the earth in respect to its nature or quality; as good land; poor land.

4. Real estate; a legal freehold. In Scripture the term carries the further sense of a covenant grant: Israel holds Canaan of the Lord, on terms, and may be evicted for breach of them.

5. The land of the living (Psa 27:13) — the sphere of present life under the sun, over against the grave; and by contrast the better country, that is, an heavenly, which the patriarchs desired (Heb 11:16).

Key Scripture

Gen 12:1 — "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:"

Lev 25:23 — "The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me."

Deu 11:12 — "A land which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year."

Heb 11:9 — "By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:"

Modern Corruption

Two errors flank the doctrine: dispensational premillennialism, which detaches a national land promise from its fulfilment in Christ and reads modern geopolitics as prophecy; and absolute private property, which forgets Lev 25:23 and treats an estate as a possession owed to no one.

expand to see more

Dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century system originating with J. N. Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible, severs Israel from the church and holds that the land promise awaits a literal national fulfilment in a future earthly millennium. No Reformation confession contains this scheme, and the New Testament reads the promise otherwise: Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he should be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), Hebrews says the patriarchs were looking past Canaan to a city with foundations (Heb 11:10, 16), and Joshua flatly records that the LORD gave Israel all the land He sware to their fathers (Jos 21:43–45). The pastoral damage of the corruption is a church reading newspapers for prophecy and treating a modern state's borders as a doctrine.

The opposite error is nearer home. Where Scripture makes every landholder a tenant — “the land is mine” — modern property theory makes him an absolute owner accountable to no one. The jubilee, the sabbath year, the gleaning laws, the redemption of a kinsman's field: every one of them presupposes that possession is stewardship and that the poor have a claim the owner may not simply refuse. This is not a socialist reading; the eighth commandment is intact and Naboth's vineyard is inviolable precisely because it is a covenant inheritance. It is the correction that ownership is real and derivative at once, and that the Owner audits.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'erets (land and earth alike) and 'adamah (tilled soil, the ground man was taken from); Greek gē and chōra; bound in the Old Testament to nachalah (inheritance) and yōbel (jubilee).

expand to see more

'erets (Hebrew, H776) — earth, land, country; the same word opens Genesis (“the heaven and the earth”) and names Canaan, so the land promise is always audibly a down payment on the whole.

'adamah (Hebrew, H127) — the arable ground, cursed for man's sake in Gen 3:17 and the source of the man's own name; the soil is a party to the Fall and to the restoration.

nachalah (Hebrew, H5159) — inheritance, the allotted portion; the tribal allotments of Joshua 13–21 are nachalah, and the word carries over to the believer's inheritance in 1Pe 1:4.

yōbel (Hebrew, H3104) — the jubilee, the fiftieth year in which every man returned to his possession (Lev 25:10); the mechanism by which the LORD's ownership was made annual and visible.

1689 London Baptist Confession 7 and 8.6 — the covenant of grace administered under both testaments with the same substance, so that the land promise is not a separate track for a separate people but a shadow of the inheritance secured in Christ.

Usage

"Because Hebrew 'erets means both land and earth, Mat 5:5 (“the meek... shall inherit the earth”) is quoting Psa 37:11 in a way that deliberately opens the smaller promise onto the larger one."

"The sabbath years were not agricultural theory. 2Ch 36:21 says the exile lasted seventy years so the land could enjoy the sabbaths Israel had refused it — a debt collected on the soil's behalf."

"Naboth's refusal to sell (1Ki 21:3) is not stubbornness but obedience to Lev 25:23; Ahab's inability to understand that refusal is the measure of how far the house of Omri had left the covenant."
